source.title: Measuring Feature Sparsity in Language Models
source.authors: Mingyang Deng; Lucas Tao; Joe Benton

page_placements.theme: Representation-level evidence of sparse, overcomplete feature structure in real models

record.tranche_reason: The study measures sparse linear representations in language-model activations, testing part of the proposed superposition mechanism with sparse-coding metrics rather than measuring polysemantic neurons directly.
record.gate_note: The study tests sparsity and linear reconstruction assumptions, not whether individual neurons respond to unrelated inputs or whether the number of features exceeds the number of neurons. Synthetic metric-validation results and token-feature examples are not direct tests of neuron polysemanticity.
record.test_reason: The study builds and validates sparse-coding metrics, then measures how well a sparse linear decomposition fits LM activations (token embeddings, BERT layer activations). This is a related but different construct. It never measures individual neurons, whether they respond to unrelated inputs, or how features compare in number with neurons; the dictionary size is fixed by the authors at 8d or 16d. So it gives no rate of polysemantic neurons and no test that superposition causes them. It relies on the superposition/sparsity framing as motivation and reports how well its own method fits. Findings go under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that LM activations across architectures and all layers are more sparse than control datasets, supporting the linearity and sparsity hypotheses, with sparsity greatest in the first and final layers. The LM comparison shown is against a Gaussian reference. They also present the work as metrics to assess sparse coding, not as a measurement of polysemantic neurons.
record.recipe_differences: Uses sparse coding and normalized-loss/average-coefficient metrics to assess activation decompositions, rather than the original neuron-visualization approach. It does not directly inspect or classify individual polysemantic neurons.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported sparsity varies across layer depth: the embedding layer is generally most sparse, sparsity decreases with depth before increasing in the latest layers, and the first and final layers are described as most sparse.

fits_no_version.finding: Token embeddings of BERT, TinyStories and GPT-Neo/GPT-2 give normalized sparse-coding loss much lower than a Gaussian reference. BERT is slightly sparser than TinyStories, and active features grow sublinearly with embedding size.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: LM activations are well modelled as sparse linear combinations of feature directions (sparsity/linearity hypotheses underlying superposition).

fits_no_version.finding: In four BERT models all layers appear sparse. Sparsity is highest at the embedding layer, decreases with depth, then rises in the final layers. At least 98% of variance is explained.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Degree of activation sparsity (superposition-friendliness) varies by layer depth, highest at first and last layers.

fits_no_version.finding: The GPT-2 'season' embedding direction mixes meanings (episodes, yearly seasons, time spans), which sparse coding splits into separate interpretable features (Appendix G, Tables 1-3).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Embedding-space directions (not neurons) superpose multiple meanings that a sparse dictionary disentangles.

record.problems: The measurements are proxies for sparse linear decomposability, not direct measurements of polysemantic neurons. The study does not establish the number of represented features relative to neuron count or test whether capacity pressure causes polysemanticity. Many language-model metric values are presented in figures without numerical values in the text.
record.rows_left_out: Individual layerwise points and variance-explained values in Figure 3(b) are not separately extracted because the provided text does not state their numerical values or layer counts; the text's qualitative all-layers result is recorded in R3-R6.

untested.parts: Share of MLP neurons responding to unrelated tokens or contexts; no neuron-level analysis.
Whether features outnumber neurons and whether this causes neuron polysemanticity. Only the sparsity/linearity assumptions of activations are probed, with an imposed dictionary size.
Polysemanticity from initialization, regularization or noise without capacity pressure.
Changes in polysemantic-neuron share with activation function, architecture or regularization. BERT vs TinyStories sparsity differences concern decomposition sparsity, not neurons.
Whether canonical polysemantic neurons detect one shared feature.
Dependence of neuron polysemanticity classification on activation range or scoring.

record.verdict_notes: No versions are tested, so no verdicts are given. The reader's V3 'supports' label is removed: the rows measure decomposability of activation vectors, not neurons, and the dictionary size is chosen by the authors. They therefore cannot show features outnumbering neurons or causing polysemanticity. Variance-explained values (R2; 98% in Appendix H) are quality checks on the authors' own method.

versions.untested_parts: Image-classifier neurons and mixed image inputs.
The share of MLP neurons responding to unrelated tokens or contexts.
Whether the number of represented features exceeds neuron count, whether features are packed into individual neurons, and whether that causes polysemanticity.
Polysemanticity from initialization, regularization, or training noise when capacity is sufficient.
Changes in polysemantic-neuron share by activation function, architecture, or regularization, and associated performance costs.
Whether canonical polysemantic neurons detect a shared feature or related offshoots rather than unrelated inputs.
Whether neuron polysemanticity classifications depend on activation range or explanation scoring.

relation.reason: Polysemantic neurons and superposition motivate the sparse-coding approach. The study tests linearity and sparsity of activations, not neurons. 'discusses' would also be acceptable.

tranche.reason: Builds and validates sparse-coding sparsity metrics, then applies them to LM activations. Never measures individual neurons or whether they are polysemantic, so it tests no version. T6 also defensible; T2 is not.

source_check.notes: Gaussian reference shown only for token embeddings (Fig 2). Fig 3 layer values are figure-only, with dictionary size 16d and per-model lambda (App. H). The study never examines individual neurons.

statements.correction: Facts in text: all layers of BERT Tiny, Mini, Small and Medium are sparse by normalized loss. General trend: the embedding layer is most sparse; sparsity decreases with depth, then rises in the latest layers. Lambda (0.0027/0.0037/0.0047/0.01) chosen to explain at least 98% of variance for all models and layers.
statements.problem: None material. The text calls the layer pattern a 'general trend' read from Fig 3. The 98% comes from choosing lambda per model (App. H).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Language-model embedding activations and BERT layer activations in the tested settings
reader_labels.reason: The sparse-coding metrics indicate sparse representations, and the embedding decompositions explain over 90% of activation variance (R1-R6); the study does not test feature-to-neuron capacity pressure or the causal explanation of polysemanticity.
